answers.answer: Caching could replace repeated 80 ms guide-building database reads with 2 ms cache lookups for popular station-language pairs. Use station:{stationId}:guide:{language}, since changing language changes the answer. On a hit, the API returns the guide stored under that key without building it in the database. On a miss, the API reads/builds the guide from the authoritative database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns it. The cache does not fetch it itself. The miss still pays the database work and wait, plus the cache lookup and cache write. Copies also use memory and require management. Weekly edits make reuse promising, though cached copies can become stale.

evidence.quote: Keeps a reusable copy of a result. Reading that copy can save database work and shorten the wait for the page.
Before a copy exists, the API still does the database lookup. Storing that copy uses memory and adds a cache write.
The API finds product:42 in the cache and returns its stored details.
The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
Include the inputs that change the answer. Reusing one person's private result for another person is a data leak.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. A fetched those hours before the commit and inserts them after B deletes the key. Deletion removes an entry at that step but does not stop the later refill of an already-fetched old value. The team cannot claim that every read after B finishes sees the new hours; C is a counterexample. A simple way to avoid this stale copy for an endpoint requiring the latest committed hours is to read the authoritative database for the response instead of returning this cached value. The prerequisite states that subsequent database reads see completed commits.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. To avoid charging an old price at checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

answers.answer: Case A: at 12:03 the request can use the original cached forecast, even though the source changed at 12:02. At 12:11 it must fetch the source because the original entry expired at 12:10. Case B: at 12:05 it must fetch the source because the cache removed the original entry at 12:04. The ten-minute TTL limits the original entry's lifetime; it does not promise freshness during that period, automatic refresh, or retention until expiry. A later miss performs the reload. Memory removal is eviction to make room and can happen before the TTL ends; expiration is the lifetime limit being reached.

evidence.quote: A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.
Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

answers.answer: One shared cache entry is the simpler fit for having a single deletion remove the map used by every instance, given no concurrent fills. Currently each local lookup happens inside that application process; deleting the writer instance's copy leaves the other instances' copies intact, so requests routed to them can still return the old map. The writer instance can miss and reload the new map while others remain old. In a shared cache all instances look up the separate cache service over the network and reuse the same entry. The cost includes the accepted 2 ms network lookup and operating the service. Losing one local cache affects that instance's copy while the other three keep theirs. An unreachable shared cache removes cache access for all four instances. Sharing itself does not automatically keep data fresh, but this single-entry deletion meets the specified goal.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold $20 while another holds $25.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.
Remove the cached entry after saving the new price in the database. A later miss reloads it.

answers.answer: When the popular key expires, many simultaneous misses can each read the same schedule from the database, exceeding its 500 reads/second capacity. Coalesce these requests so one database lookup runs and concurrent readers share its result rather than each starting a lookup. During a whole-cache outage, forwarding all 10,000 requests/second to the database would exceed capacity by twenty times. Limit fallback database reads to at most the safe 500/second, and return a temporary error for excess work. If an accessible last known schedule is available and satisfies the permitted 60-second age, return it instead of starting database reads; otherwise reject excess requests. This keeps fallback work within database capacity and older permitted responses avoid database work altogether. Do not assume an unreachable cache can supply that older copy.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.
A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Each unique result is read only once, so filling the cache after its database read produces no future hit and saves no database lookup. The existing 2 ms read is comfortably within the 100 ms budget, and ten reads/second is comfortably within capacity. The cache would add writes and memory use, plus managing another copy, without reuse benefit. Reconsider if the same result IDs begin receiving many repeat reads, especially if repeated database work becomes a meaningful latency or capacity concern.

First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track the fraction of lookups that hit, and what happens during misses.
